summary: Describes the Internet Control Message Protocol, which lets gateways and hosts report errors and exchange simple diagnostic information about how datagrams are handled. This early edition was replaced by the final specification. Replaced by RFC 792.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMP lets gateways and hosts report some problems with IP datagrams and exchange simple diagnostic messages. It does not make IP reliable, and RFC 777 was later replaced by RFC 792.

subtitle: Control messages that report errors and conditions in IP datagram delivery

tldr.problem: IP datagrams can fail during delivery, but IP itself does not guarantee delivery or report every loss.
tldr.mechanism: ICMP lets gateways and hosts send control messages to a datagram's source, including error reports, redirects and diagnostic replies.
tldr.outcome: RFC 777 is an early ICMP specification and was later replaced by RFC 792.

facts.label: Original data included in error reports

sections.title: Purpose of ICMP
sections.content:
The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is used by gateways and hosts to report errors in processing IP datagrams and to exchange control information. The RFC describes ICMP as an integral part of IP, even though ICMP messages use IP to travel.

ICMP provides feedback, not guaranteed delivery. A datagram may be lost without a control message, and higher-level protocols must provide their own reliability if they need it. To avoid an endless chain of reports, ICMP messages are not sent about ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP reports some problems that happen while IP datagrams are handled. It does not guarantee that a message or its report will arrive.

sections.title: Message Structure and Types
sections.content:
An ICMP message is carried using the IP header, with IP protocol number 1. The first octet of the IP data is an ICMP type; the type determines the rest of the message format. Error messages include the original Internet header and the first 64 bits of the original datagram's data so the host can match the report to a process.

This version lists Destination Unreachable, Source Quench, Redirect, Echo, Echo Reply, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem, Timestamp and Timestamp Reply. The messages report delivery problems, ask a sender to reduce its rate, suggest a gateway, or support diagnostic exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte says what kind of ICMP message follows. Some types report errors; others request or return diagnostic information.

sections.title: When Gateways and Hosts Send Reports
sections.content:
A gateway may report that a destination network is unreachable. A destination host may report that a requested protocol or port is not active. A gateway must discard a datagram that needs fragmentation when the Don't Fragment flag is set, and must return a Destination Unreachable message.

A gateway may report that a datagram's time-to-live reached zero, and a host may report that fragment reassembly exceeded its time limit. A gateway or host may send Source Quench when it discards data or approaches its capacity, asking the source to reduce its sending rate. A Redirect advises a host to send traffic through a more direct gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Different conditions produce different reports, such as an unreachable destination, a time limit, or a better route. Source Quench asks the sender to slow down when a gateway or host is under pressure.
